editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We present an embedding of a 61-vertex, 5-chromatic graph of girth 4 in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) as a unit-distance graph (UDG). We speculate that no 6-chromatic case exists, even though 6-chromatic UDGs in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with girth 3 exist having as few as 47 vertices. However, our discovery provides motivation to seek 5-chromatic cases with larger girth, not least because there exist 4-chromatic unit-distance graphs in the plane with arbitrary girth.

title.title: A 5-chromatic, triangle-free unit-distance graph in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with 61 vertices

editorial_contributions.text: The problem of determining the minimum number of colors that are needed to color the points of the plane so that no two points unit distance apart are assigned the same color is considered. This number is referred to as the chromatic number of the plane denoted by \(\chi(\mathbb{E}^2)\). One of the problems that prevailed in the literature is ``What is the smallest order of a 4-chromatic unit distance graphs of girth 4?''. In this article, the authors construct triangle-free 4-chromatic unit distance graphs with 21, 19, and 17 vertices. The authors present an evidence that the value 17 cannot be improved.

The author introduces a class of 4-chromatic graphs with large girth and promises to prove in the second part of the paper that these graphs are unit distance graphs.

title.title: Arbitrary girth, 4-chromatic unit distance graphs in the plane. ~I: Graph description

editorial_contributions.text:
Erdős' unit distance problem, which is still wide open, asks how many unit distances may occur among \(n\) points in the plane. Borsuk's (refuted) conjecture asserted that any set of diameter 1 in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) can be partitioned into \(d+1\) subsets of smaller diameter. These problems, and many other, can be put conveniently in terms of distance graphs. A distance graph in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is represented by a set of points corresponding to the vertices, and all edges correspond to pairs of vertices at distance \(a\). The distance graph is complete, if all pairs of points at distance \(a\) correspond to an edge. Hadwiger and Nelson found that the complete unit distance graph with vertex set \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has its chromatic number between 4 and 7 -- and no better bounds have been found yet. Corroborating a conjecture of Erdős, the chromatic number of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) grows exponentially. The paper under review investigates variants of the distance graph problems above under additional assumptions like on girth, on odd girth, on number of cliques of given size, or for distance graphs represented by a spherical vertex set. Many of the results in the exposition are from the author of the paper.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1297.00036].
